questions.q: A 28-year-old man from rural Bihar presents with a hypopigmented anaesthetic patch on his left forearm with a thickened ulnar nerve. Slit-skin smear is negative. The MOST likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: BT leprosy presents with one or few (2-5) hypopigmented anaesthetic patches with clearly defined margins, associated peripheral nerve thickening, and negative/low BI. It falls on the tuberculoid end of the spectrum.

questions.q: A leprosy patient on MDT develops sudden acute painful swelling of existing skin lesions with new erythematous plaques, fever, and iridocyclitis. The MOST appropriate immediate management is:
questions.exp: Type 1 reaction (reversal reaction) in leprosy is managed by continuing MDT and adding prednisolone (40-60 mg/day tapering over 3-6 months). MDT must never be stopped as it treats the underlying infection.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with flaccid blisters on her back and chest that rupture easily leaving raw erosions. Nikolsky sign is positive. Direct immunofluorescence shows intercellular IgG deposition in a 'chicken-wire' pattern. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris presents with flaccid blisters, positive Nikolsky sign, and DIF showing intercellular IgG deposition (fish-net/chicken-wire pattern) due to antibodies against desmoglein 3 (and 1 in mucocutaneous disease).

questions.q: A 65-year-old man presents with tense bullae on erythematous base over the abdomen and thighs. Nikolsky sign is negative. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 deposition at the dermoepidermal junction. The target antigen is most likely:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid is characterized by tense bullae, negative Nikolsky sign, and linear IgG/C3 at the DEJ on DIF. The major antigen is BP180 (BPAG2, type XVII collagen) and BP230 (BPAG1).

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with intensely pruritic vesicles symmetrically distributed over elbows, knees, and buttocks. Skin biopsy shows subepidermal blister with neutrophils at dermal papillae. The MOST specific test to confirm the diagnosis is:
opts: Perilesional DIF showing granular IgA at dermal papillae
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is confirmed by perilesional DIF showing granular IgA deposits at dermal papillae tips. It is associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathy. Serum anti-endomysial and anti-tTG antibodies support the diagnosis but DIF is most specific for skin.

questions.q: A 30-year-old HIV-positive patient presents with extensive whitish curd-like plaques on the oral mucosa that can be scraped off, leaving an erythematous base. KOH mount shows pseudohyphae. The FIRST-LINE treatment is:
questions.exp: Oropharyngeal candidiasis in HIV patients is treated with oral fluconazole 100-200 mg/day for 7-14 days. Topical nystatin is used for mild cases in immunocompetent patients; systemic fluconazole is preferred in immunocompromised individuals.

questions.q: A 20-year-old student presents with hypopigmented, finely scaling macules on the chest and upper back, more prominent in summer. Wood's lamp shows yellow-green fluorescence. The causative organism is:
questions.exp: Pityriasis (tinea) versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur (and M. globosa). It presents with hypo/hyperpigmented scaly macules, yellow-green fluorescence on Wood's lamp, and 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance on KOH (short hyphae + spores).

questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a painless papule on his right hand that ulcerated and developed a black eschar with surrounding edema. He had contact with cattle. The MOST likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Cutaneous anthrax (caused by Bacillus anthracis) presents as a painless papule progressing to a black eschar (malignant pustule) surrounded by edema, following contact with infected animals or animal products. Treatment is penicillin or ciprofloxacin.

questions.q: A 5-year-old child develops honey-coloured crusted lesions around the nose and mouth. Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters. The MOST common causative organism is:
questions.exp: Non-bullous impetigo is predominantly caused by Staphylococcus aureus (also S. pyogenes). Honey-coloured crusts form after rupture of vesicles/pustules. Bullous impetigo is exclusively caused by S. aureus phage type 71 producing exfoliative toxin.

questions.q: A 24-year-old sexually active woman presents with multiple painful genital ulcers with undermined edges and a soft base. Inguinal lymph nodes are tender. Gram stain of ulcer material shows 'school of fish' pattern. The causative organism is:
questions.exp: Chancroid (caused by Haemophilus ducreyi) presents with painful soft ulcers with undermined edges, tender inguinal lymphadenopathy (bubo), and Gram stain showing 'school of fish' or 'railway tracks' pattern of Gram-negative coccobacilli.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with a painless indurated ulcer on his glans penis. VDRL is positive 1:16. The PRIMARY treatment of choice is:
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose
questions.exp: Primary syphilis (Treponema pallidum) is treated with benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose. This is the drug of choice. Doxycycline is used for penicillin-allergic patients.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with painless genital ulcers and beefy-red granulation tissue. Tissue smear shows Donovan bodies (encapsulated Gram-negative bacilli in mononuclear cells). The diagnosis and treatment of choice are:
questions.exp: Granuloma inguinale (Donovanosis), caused by Klebsiella granulomatis, presents with progressive painless ulcers with beefy-red granulation and Donovan bodies on smear. First-line treatment is azithromycin 1 g weekly or 500 mg daily for minimum 3 weeks.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with recurrent painful grouped vesicles on an erythematous base on her labia. Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. The MOST appropriate treatment for suppression of recurrences is:
questions.exp: For suppressive therapy of recurrent genital herpes (HSV-2), valacyclovir 500 mg once daily (or acyclovir 400 mg BD) is used continuously. Suppressive therapy reduces frequency of recurrences by 70-80% and also reduces asymptomatic viral shedding.

questions.q: A 40-year-old immunosuppressed patient develops painful grouped vesicles along the left T5 dermatome with post-herpetic neuralgia. The antiviral agent MOST effective in reducing postherpetic neuralgia when given within 72 hours is:
questions.exp: Famciclovir (prodrug of penciclovir) has been shown to be most effective in reducing the duration and incidence of postherpetic neuralgia in clinical trials compared to acyclovir. It achieves higher intracellular penciclovir concentrations and has longer intracellular half-life.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with photosensitive facial rash in a butterfly distribution, oral ulcers, and arthritis. ANA is positive (1:640). Anti-dsDNA antibodies are strongly positive. The skin biopsy shows 'lupus band' on DIF. The cutaneous manifestation most specific for SLE is:
questions.exp: The malar (butterfly) rash of SLE is an acute cutaneous manifestation highly specific for SLE. It spares the nasolabial folds. Discoid lupus can occur without systemic disease. The lupus band test (IgG, IgM, C3 at DEJ) in non-lesional sun-exposed skin is positive in ~50-60% of SLE.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman presents with proximal muscle weakness, heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules over knuckles, and V-sign erythema on the chest. The MOST important investigation to screen for internal malignancy is:
opts: CT scan of chest, abdomen, and pelvis
questions.exp: Dermatomyositis (especially in adults >40 years) is associated with internal malignancy in 15-30% of cases. CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis is the most appropriate screening investigation. Anti-Jo-1 is associated with antisynthetase syndrome with ILD rather than malignancy.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with tight, bound-down skin over face and hands with Raynaud's phenomenon and dysphagia. ANA is positive with anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) antibody. This antibody is most associated with:
opts: Limited systemic sclerosis with pulmonary hypertension
Diffuse systemic sclerosis with pulmonary fibrosis
questions.exp: Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) antibody is associated with diffuse systemic sclerosis and carries a high risk for pulmonary fibrosis and poor prognosis. Anti-centromere antibodies are associated with limited systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome) and pulmonary hypertension.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with an ulcerated pearly nodule with rolled edges and telangiectasias on his nose, with 20 years of sun exposure. Histology shows palisading nuclei, retraction artifact, and peripheral palisading. The PRIMARY treatment with the highest cure rate for this lesion is:
questions.exp: Mohs micrographic surgery achieves the highest cure rate (99%) for primary basal cell carcinoma (BCC) on high-risk sites (face, particularly nose, periorbital). It allows complete margin assessment and maximal tissue conservation.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man with xeroderma pigmentosum develops a rapidly growing keratinous nodule on his lower lip that bleeds on contact. Histology shows atypical squamous cells with keratin pearls and stromal invasion. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is positive. This represents:
opts: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) with nodal metastasis
questions.exp: SCC can metastasize to regional lymph nodes; the lip is a high-risk site. XP patients have markedly increased risk of UV-induced skin cancers. Keratin pearls are characteristic of well-differentiated SCC. Positive SLNB indicates nodal spread requiring neck dissection ± adjuvant therapy.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with an asymmetric pigmented lesion on her back, 1.2 cm diameter, with irregular borders, variegated color (tan, brown, black), and a notch. Dermoscopy shows atypical pigment network, blue-white veil, and irregular dots/globules. Breslow thickness on excision is 2.1 mm. The staging (T stage) is:
questions.exp: AJCC melanoma T-staging: T3 = 2.01–4.0 mm Breslow thickness. T3a = without ulceration, T3b = with ulceration. At 2.1 mm without ulceration, this is T3a. T1 ≤1.0 mm; T2 = 1.01–2.0 mm.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with well-defined erythematous silvery scaly plaques on elbows, knees, and scalp with nail pitting. Histology shows acanthosis, elongated rete ridges, parakeratosis, and Munro's microabscesses. The cytokine MOST central to the pathogenesis is:
questions.exp: IL-17A (from Th17 cells), driven by IL-23 from dendritic cells, is the most central cytokine in psoriasis pathogenesis. The IL-23/IL-17 axis is the main therapeutic target. Biologics targeting IL-17A (secukinumab, ixekizumab) and IL-23 (guselkumab, risankizumab) are highly effective.

questions.q: A 35-year-old psoriasis patient develops joint pain, stiffness, and sacroiliac involvement. The HLA type most strongly associated with psoriatic arthritis with axial involvement is:
questions.exp: HLA-B27 is strongly associated with psoriatic arthritis with axial (spondylitic) involvement and uveitis. HLA-Cw6 is associated with guttate/early-onset psoriasis. HLA-B13, B17 are associated with plaque psoriasis.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman on oral contraceptive pills develops a fixed drug eruption over her lips after taking co-trimoxazole. The medication is stopped. The characteristic histological finding in a fixed drug eruption is:
opts: Interface dermatitis with apoptotic keratinocytes and pigment incontinence
Perivascular eosinophilic infiltrate with flame figures
Acantholysis with tombstone row of basal cells
questions.exp: Fixed drug eruption histology shows interface dermatitis with apoptotic (necrotic) keratinocytes, basal cell vacuolation, and melanophages (pigment incontinence) in the upper dermis — explaining the residual hyperpigmentation. CD8+ T cells are resident in the epidermis.

questions.q: A 20-year-old man on carbamazepine for epilepsy develops widespread erythematous macules coalescing over >30% BSA with epidermal detachment, erosions of mucous membranes at 3 sites, and positive Nikolsky sign. The IMMEDIATE most critical management step is:
opts: Transfer to burn ICU, stop offending drug, supportive care
questions.exp: Stevens-Johnson syndrome/Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (SJS/TEN) with >30% BSA detachment is TEN. The immediate priority is stopping the causative drug, transferring to a specialized burn/ICU unit, and providing supportive care (wound care, fluid/electrolyte management, nutrition, eye care). Controversy exists about IVIG and cyclosporine; supportive care is the established first step.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with tinea capitis showing a kerion — boggy, inflamed mass with pustules on the scalp — and occipital lymphadenopathy. The MOST common causative organism of kerion in India is:
questions.exp: In India, Trichophyton violaceum and T. tonsurans (endothrix) are the most common causes of tinea capitis and kerion. T. violaceum is the predominant species in India. Kerion is an immunological reaction to dermatophyte antigens; treatment is oral griseofulvin or terbinafine plus short-course steroids.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man presents with recurrent urticaria for more than 6 weeks. Physical examination and routine investigations are normal. The MOST appropriate next step in management is:
opts: Second-generation non-sedating antihistamine at standard dose
questions.exp: Chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) first-line treatment is a second-generation H1 antihistamine (cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine) at licensed dose. Routine extensive allergy workup is not recommended in CSU as it is usually idiopathic. Systemic steroids are reserved for acute exacerbations.

questions.q: A 19-year-old presents with comedones, inflammatory papules/pustules, and a few nodules on face and upper back. He has been using topical benzoyl peroxide for 6 weeks without improvement. The NEXT appropriate step is:
opts: Add oral doxycycline 100 mg BD plus topical retinoid
questions.exp: For moderate acne (papules, pustules, nodules) failing topical monotherapy, guidelines recommend oral antibiotics (doxycycline/tetracycline) COMBINED with a topical retinoid. Combination reduces antibiotic resistance. Isotretinoin is reserved for severe nodulo-cystic acne or treatment failure.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman on oral isotretinoin for nodulocystic acne asks about pregnancy. The teratogenic effect of isotretinoin is MOST closely related to its effect on:
opts: Retinoic acid receptors in cephalic neural crest cells
questions.exp: Isotretinoin (13-cis retinoic acid) is a potent teratogen acting via retinoic acid receptors in cephalic neural crest cells, causing craniofacial malformations, CNS defects, cardiovascular defects, and thymic aplasia. iPLEDGE (US) and similar risk management programs require two forms of contraception.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with multiple flesh-colored papules on the perianal area and penile shaft. Aceto-whitening is positive. Histology shows koilocytes with nuclear atypia. The HPV types MOST likely responsible are:
questions.exp: Condylomata acuminata (anogenital warts) are caused by low-risk HPV types 6 and 11, which rarely progress to malignancy. High-risk types (16, 18, 31, 33) are associated with cervical/anogenital carcinoma. HPV 1, 2, 4 cause common/plantar warts.

questions.q: A skin biopsy from a psoriatic plaque is processed for immunohistochemistry. The cell that is considered the PRIMARY initiating antigen-presenting cell in the pathogenesis of psoriasis is:
questions.exp: Myeloid/conventional dendritic cells (mDCs) are the primary initiating APCs in psoriasis. Activated mDCs produce IL-12 and IL-23, driving Th1 and Th17 differentiation respectively. Plasmacytoid DCs produce IFN-α early in disease initiation. Langerhans cells have a lesser role compared to dermal DCs.

questions.q: During dermoscopy evaluation of a suspicious pigmented lesion, which dermoscopic feature is MOST specific for melanoma diagnosis:
opts: Regression structures (white scar-like areas + blue pepper-like granules)
questions.exp: Regression structures in dermoscopy (white scar-like depigmentation combined with blue-grey pepper-like granules/peppering) are highly specific for melanoma. They represent fibrosis and melanophages from regressed tumor areas. Milia-like cysts are benign (seborrhoeic keratosis); comma vessels suggest dermal nevus.
